chapter: Ellington's later years and Quincy Jones
title: Outswinging Stan Kenton at the Graystone
summary: Woodyard rallied the band to put the pots on, and Ellington's band swung all night while Kenton's men stood astounded.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: There's some beautiful stories about that band, too. We played the Graystone with Stan Kenton and that band swung all night long. They took us out of the ballroom and put us in the garden and the people were screaming when we finished there. And Stan asked his band to leave and they wouldn't leave. We was playing the last set. And we swung all night long and we didn't play the greatest thing, "Diminuendo and Crescendo", till the very last tune. We didn't even need it.

And I knew that the band was going to swing that night because when we was dressing out there in the bus to go in the ballroom, Sam Woodyard spoke up and said, "Look," he said, "fellows, we're going to put the pots on tonight." I said, "Oh, oh." I said, "Oh, oh." So we did. He put the pots on. Yes, he did. And when Stan was trying to get his band to leave the cats were looking at us with their mouth open. They wouldn't even leave to go out and get in their bus, they were so astounded, like everybody else in the Graystone was astounded. Anybody that would want to play against Duke Ellington's band would become astounded, because I've seen this band sometimes they would get lax, just like any other band, you know, --
-- and wouldn't play, but don't push them. Don't push them. My dear.
